title: What uses electricity at home
keyIdea: Many things at home need electricity to work. Some plug into a wall socket and use mains electricity. Others, like a torch or a remote, use batteries. Anything that lights up, heats, moves, makes a sound or shows a screen is using electricity. Things that do none of those, such as a wooden spoon, a book or a blanket, do not need electricity. Spotting which things use electricity is the first step before learning about circuits and using electricity safely.

kid: Look around your home. A lamp shines. A kettle gets hot. A fan spins. A radio makes a sound. A tablet shows a picture. All of these use electricity.
Some things plug into a hole in the wall. That is called mains electricity. A fridge, a TV and a toaster use mains electricity.
Other things use batteries. A torch, a remote control and many toys run on batteries. The electricity is stored inside the battery.
A wooden spoon, a book and a blanket do not light up, heat, move, make a sound or show a screen. They do not need electricity.
adult: In the National Curriculum for England, Year 4 Electricity asks pupils to identify common appliances that run on electricity. This lesson is the naming step before circuits, conductors and switches. It sits beside, but does not replace, 'Using electricity safely' (mains dangers) and 'Circuit words' (components, series and parallel).

The useful split is mains versus battery, then a check that the thing actually does electrical work: light, heat, movement, sound or a screen. A wind-up toy moves without electricity. A candle gives light and heat from burning, not from a plug or a battery.

Common mistakes: thinking everything that moves uses electricity (a scooter does not), thinking a battery is the same as a plug, and listing a plug itself as an appliance. Some children think a phone 'has no electricity' when it is off. The power is still there, waiting.

In the lab your child sorts room items into uses electricity or not, then into plug or battery. They tap an appliance to name the job it does with electricity, and spot three fakes that look electrical but are not.

familyTip: Walk from room to room and play 'plug, battery or neither'. Point at a lamp, a remote, a clock, a broom and a phone charger. Ask which need electricity and where it comes from. Unplug nothing that is in use; just look and talk.

visual.caption: Does it need electricity? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: sort what uses electricity, split plug from battery, name the job each appliance does, and spot three fakes that do not use electricity.

practice.prompt: Which of these needs electricity to work?
practice.hint: Which one keeps food cold using a motor and a plug?
practice.explain: A fridge plugs into the wall and uses electricity to keep food cold. A spoon and a blanket do not.

practice.prompt: A torch usually gets its electricity from…
practice.hint: You put small cells inside a torch.
practice.explain: A torch runs on batteries. A wall socket is mains electricity. Burning wax is a candle, not a torch.

practice.prompt: Which list is all mains appliances?
practice.hint: Mains means plugged into a wall socket.
practice.explain: A toaster, a TV and a washing machine all plug into the wall. Torches and remotes use batteries. Books, candles and brooms need no electricity.

practice.prompt: A kitchen has {a} plugged-in appliances and {b} battery toys. How many things use electricity?
practice.hint: Add the plugged-in ones and the battery ones.

practice.prompt: A living room has {a} lamps on plugs and {b} battery remotes. How many use electricity?
practice.hint: Lamps on plugs and remotes on batteries both use electricity. Add them.

pool.hint: A candle burns wax. Say why, using plug, battery or neither.
pool.explain: A candle gives light by burning, not by electricity. A lamp and a phone both need electricity.

pool.hint: Think of the holes in the wall you plug into.
pool.explain: Mains electricity comes through wall sockets. Batteries are separate. The sun can make electricity via solar panels, but that is not what 'mains' means at home.

pool.prompt: A remote control usually runs on…
pool.hint: You open the back and put small cells in.
pool.explain: Most remotes use AA or AAA batteries. They do not plug into the wall.

pool.hint: Which one has a motor?. Say why, using plug, battery or neither.
pool.explain: A fan's motor needs electricity to spin. A broom and a book do not.

pool.prompt: You find {a} plug sockets in use and {b} battery devices on. How many electrical things are on?
pool.hint: Count both kinds. Say why, using plug, battery or neither.

pool.prompt: A phone that is switched off…
choices: still stores electricity in its battery
pool.hint: What happens when you press the power button?
pool.explain: The battery still holds chemical energy that can become electrical energy when you switch it on.

pool.hint: Which one do you carry without a cable?
pool.explain: A torch runs on batteries. A washing machine and a wall lamp use mains electricity.

pool.prompt: Sam says a scooter uses electricity because it moves. Is Sam right?
choices: No, a push scooter moves without electricity
Yes, all moving things use electricity
pool.hint: Does a push scooter have a motor or a battery?
pool.explain: A push scooter moves because you push it. Only an electric scooter with a battery uses electricity.

pool.prompt: Room A has {a} electrical things and room B has {b}. How many in both rooms?
pool.hint: Add the electrical things in room A to the ones in room B.
